articles.title: Platform Peers: The Little-Known Market for Peer Reviews
articles.authors: Amna Pottarath; Willem Halffman; Serge P. J. M. Horbach
articles.abstract: Paid peer review has long been proposed as a solution to reviewer fatigue, but seemed to remain little implemented in practice. In this article we examine the not-so-visible market for paid peer review through website analysis and qualitative interviews, demonstrating the practice is commonplace in some parts of the industry. The ethos of community service is fading, as peer review in this context is increasingly becoming an immediate, time-bound transaction, often completed within 2-3 days. We therefore focus on issues of opacity, exploring who pays whom, as well as the motivations and perspectives of reviewers who receive payment.

articles.title: Transforming Research through Open Data: A Cyclical Model for Emerging Data-Driven Research
articles.authors: Honami Numajiri; Thed N van Leeuwen; Takayuki Hayashi
articles.abstract: As open science has become institutionalised worldwide, open data are now viewed not only as transparency mechanisms but also as a foundation for data-driven research. However, their effects on researcher practices remain insufficiently understood. This study examines how researchers use open data and its impact on research practices across disciplines. Building on prior theories of scientific field development, we developed a cyclical impact model in which open data transform research practices and foster data sharing. We applied this model to 183 valid survey responses from researchers affiliated with institutions in Japan whose publications cited items indexed in the Data Citation Index. The results revealed that open-data users more frequently reported comparative analysis, efficient use of research funds, and big-data analysis than non-users. Latent class analysis identified five cross-disciplinary usage patterns: Interdisciplinary Foundation, Big Data Exploration, Comprehensive Integration, Standard Information, and Social Implementation. Among them, Big Data Exploration and Interdisciplinary Foundation appear as key drivers of the emerging ‘data-driven research’ paradigm, where knowledge creation increasingly depends on reusing, integrating, and sharing data across traditional boundaries. High data-sharing rates across all classes support the cyclical model, in which open data usage encourages further sharing, driving methodological innovation and reinforcing openness and discovery. These findings suggest that policy and institutional support should prioritise sustaining this cycle of data use and sharing by fostering diverse modes of open-data utilisation rather than relying on traditional disciplinary boundaries.

articles_hidden.title: Outcome definitions in clinical trial registrations: a cross-sectional study
articles_hidden.authors: Kiran Ninan; Jean-Pierre Oberste; Xiangji Ying; Nicholas J DeVito; Tianjing Li; David Blanco; Carolina Grana; Isabelle Boutron; Carrie Baldwin-SoRelle; Halil Kilicoglu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Importance: Defining outcomes completely in trial registrations limits opportunities for reporting bias. That is, an incomplete outcome definition might be compatible with multiple results, so investigators could conduct many analyses and calculate different effects that would all appear to be consistent with the planned outcome. 

Objective: To evaluate outcome definitions for registered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to determine whether they were complete or incomplete.

Design: A cross-sectional study of RCTs registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and published in International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) member journals from 1 January to 30 June, 2025. 

Setting: ClinicalTrials.gov and RCTs published in ICMJE member journals.

Participants: Outcomes registered before or soon after participant enrollment began for eligible RCTs.

Exposure: This study characterized outcome registration completeness without a formal exposure or intervention.

Main Outcomes and Measures: The proportion of outcomes that were defined completely (i.e., included a specific measurement, specific metric, variable type, time point, and cutoff, if applicable). Results were explored by outcome priority (i.e., Primary, Secondary, Other outcomes), trial regulatory status for RCTs governed by the US Food and Drug Administration Amendments Act (i.e., “Applicable Clinical Trials” versus other RCTs), by funder (i.e., Industry, National Institutes of Health, Other governmental organizations, Other), and journal.

Results: Among 210 RCTs including 2543 registered outcomes, only 6 RCTs (2.9%) defined all outcomes completely and 326 outcomes (12.8%) were defined completely. Most outcomes defined the specific measurement (72.7%) and metric (85.7%), and the cutoff where applicable (65.0%) but not variable type (22.4%). In exploratory analyses, outcome definitions were more complete for Primary outcomes compared with Secondary and Other outcomes (20.5% versus 12.2% and 9.2%, respectively). Outcomes in Applicable Clinical Trials were better defined than outcomes in other RCTs (15.5% versus 11.0%), and outcomes in RCTs sponsored by Industry or funded by the National Institutes of Health were better defined than outcomes in Other RCTs (17.0% and 19.6% versus 7.4%, respectively). There was no evidence of differences across journals.

Conclusions and Relevance: Most RCTs published in ICMJE member journals did not define their outcomes completely in registrations. Complete outcome definitions in trial registrations could prevent reporting biases.

articles_hidden.title: Replicating a preclinical systematic review and meta-analysis: a case study of the antidepressant-like effects of minocycline in rodents
articles_hidden.authors: Matheus Gallas-Lopes; Daniela Varisco Müller; Bruno Dutra Arbo; Angelo Piato; Ana Paula Herrmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: The reproducibility of preclinical systematic reviews and meta-analyses remains underexplored, particularly when key review decisions are not fully recoverable from the published record. We conducted a direct replication of a published systematic review and meta-analysis on the antidepressant-like effects of minocycline in rodents, complemented by a computational reproduction based on the dataset of the original study. Methods: Searches were performed in PubMed and Web of Science, and study selection, data extraction, and SYRCLE risk of bias assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers. Effect sizes were synthesised using robust variance estimation. Results: We identified 30 potentially eligible studies, including 21 recovered from the original review and nine additional studies. After excluding two studies from the primary quantitative synthesis, 28 studies were retained in the direct replication dataset. The direct replication yielded a somewhat larger pooled effect than the original review (Hedges’ g = −1.21, 95% CI −1.51 to −0.91, compared with g = −1.07, 95% CI −1.41 to −0.74), whereas the computational reproduction matched the published estimate (g = −1.07, 95% CI −1.41 to −0.74). Sensitivity analyses attenuated the estimate but did not alter its direction (risk of bias-adjusted g = −1.06; animal recycling-adjusted g = −0.95). Funnel-plot asymmetry and Egger’s regressions suggested small-study effects. Risk of bias agreement with the original review was limited in several domains, particularly incomplete outcome data and blinding-related domains. Although the direction of the pooled effect was preserved, incomplete reporting of the original workflow required independent decisions regarding search implementation, eligibility assessment, outcome handling, and risk of bias judgments. Conclusions: This replication supports the view that the preclinical literature is broadly consistent with an antidepressant-like effect of minocycline in rodents. However, the magnitude of this effect should be interpreted cautiously in light of small-study effects, methodological limitations, and incomplete transparency in the review workflow.

articles_hidden.title: Data and Code Availability in Sports Science: A Registered Report
articles_hidden.authors: Simon Nolte; Daniel Memmert; Robert Rein
articles_hidden.abstract: Sharing scientific raw data and analysis code facilitates cumulative scientific work and enables assessments of reproducibility and robustness. In sports science, preliminary evidence suggests that data and code availability may be low, but previous studies have been based on small cross-sectional samples. To provide a larger audit of the literature, we will document data and code sharing in all original articles published in Q1 sport science journals over the past ten years. We will calculate the percentages of reported as well as actual public availability of data and code and investigate whether general time trends exist. Data and code sharing policies of the analyzed journals will be surveyed to examine associations between policy changes and sharing rates. We provide a resource with all articles in the sample that have shared data and/or code for reuse. The findings of this study can be used to inform future data and code sharing policies in sport science.
